The web version, installed like an app
Many services also exist as a website. Your browser can install it on the home screen: it then has its own icon and opens full screen, like an app. This is a WebAPK.

What you gain: the native app and its permissions go away, and so do the trackers built into its code. The site runs in your browser, which only gives it what you accept, and the DNS filtering applies to it.
What you may lose, depending on the site: some notifications, offline use, a few features specific to the app.
VYLIA cannot measure a website\'s trackers, so it shows no score for the web version. A browser that blocks trackers adds to the gain.
Your apps that have a website

VYLIA Shield: your DNS requests are filtered on the phone, then the allowed ones go unencrypted to your network\'s DNS.
Encryption stops your Internet provider, or the public Wi-Fi you are on, from seeing the list of services your phone contacts, a list that says a lot about you.

Limits, for the Shield as for private DNS: a tracker that shares its server with the app itself cannot be blocked without breaking the app, and neither stops tracking through an account you are signed in to.
DNS is the Internet\'s directory: it turns a site name, like example.org, into the address your phone connects to.
By default these requests go through your Internet provider unencrypted, so it can see which sites and services your apps contact.
Private DNS encrypts them (DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS). Depending on the service, it can also block malicious domains or trackers.
You turn it on once in the settings, and it protects every app on the phone.
It is not a VPN: it does not hide your IP address and does not make your browsing anonymous. The sites you visit still see your address.

These apps come from AlternativeTo, a site where people recommend alternatives to one another. In each category, VYLIA keeps the free apps that users like most, available on Android, and opens their Google Play page (or F-Droid if there is none). It reflects popularity, not an audit: their score appears in VYLIA once you install them. The rating shown is the one on Google Play, when the app is there.
Before contacting a tracker\'s server, an app asks for its address (a DNS request). Refusing to answer that request stops the data from being sent, for every app at once. Two tools can do it:

• VYLIA Shield: the filtering is done on the phone, with VYLIA\'s lists. One switch, a choice between web and mobile filtering, a pause, and a live counter. It uses a local VPN (Android allows only one VPN at a time) and does not encrypt the requests it lets through.

• Private DNS: your requests are encrypted and sent to a service you choose, set once in Android\'s settings, with no VPN. It only blocks trackers if that service filters them (NextDNS can, Quad9 does not), and the service sees your requests.

Use one or the other: when private DNS is set to a service, Android sends it the requests directly and the Shield sees none of them. To block trackers simply, choose the Shield; to also encrypt your requests, choose a private DNS that filters (NextDNS).
Blocks the tracking requests of all your apps, right on the phone.
Stopped: another VPN took over. Android only allows one at a time.

How it works: VYLIA creates a VPN on the phone itself. Only DNS requests (the Internet\'s directory) go through it: those for known tracking servers are refused, the others go on to your network\'s usual DNS. Nothing is sent to a VYLIA server, and the rest of your traffic does not go through VYLIA.
Private DNS is set to %1$s: Android then sends its requests straight to that service and the Shield sees none of them. Choose one or the other: to use the Shield, set private DNS back to Automatic.
Another VPN is on: turning on the Shield will replace it.
Limits: apps that encrypt their own DNS (some browsers) bypass the Shield, and blocking a tracker can occasionally break a feature: if an app misbehaves, turn the Shield off.

To keep it on after a restart, turn on “Always-on VPN” for VYLIA in Android\'s VPN settings, but leave “Block connections without VPN” off: the Shield only carries DNS, so that option would cut off the Internet.

resources.string: The main families of trackers, what they do with your data and the most common ones. A tracker can belong to several families: the most serious one counts in the score.
Tap a permission to see what it allows, why it is sensitive and how it is granted.
The Privacy Score at a glance

Every app starts with %1$d points. It loses points for the permissions it requests and the trackers it embeds, and spying capabilities can cap its score. Everything is computed on your phone, offline.
The algorithm is open source and the rules it applies are in Settings › Scoring rules: you can export them, edit them and import them back.

The permission penalty is not the same for every app: it depends on what the app is for. GPS costs nothing to a navigation app, which needs it, but costs a lot to a game, which has no reason to use it (details in 1 and 3 below).
The caps keep a single aspect from crushing everything: an app never loses more than %1$d points for its permissions nor more than %2$d for its trackers.
The grade and its risk level
A “%1$s” after the grade (e.g. %2$s) marks a provisional score: the trackers could not be analysed yet.
Each counted permission has a weight according to its severity: from %1$d (%2$s) to %3$d (%4$s). This weight is then adjusted by two questions.
Is it related to what the app does? (context)
Justified (×%1$s): needed for the feature, e.g. GPS for a navigation app.
Unexpected (×%1$s): no obvious link with the app\'s category.
Forbidden (×%1$s): no justification at all, e.g. contacts for a game.
A granted permission counts in full. A permission that is only declared (the app plans for it but you have not accepted it) counts ×%1$s: it remains a sign of intent.
Precise location weighs %1$d. Granted to a navigation app, where it is justified: %1$d × %2$s = 0 points lost. Granted to a game, where it is forbidden: %1$d × %3$s = %4$s points lost.
Capabilities that depend on an access

Some permissions are useless on their own. Running the microphone, camera or location in the background requires that access to be granted first; until then they count ×%1$s. Screen capture needs your consent every time, so it always counts ×%1$s.

Ad targeting permissions (advertising ID, Android\'s ad services) are not counted here: advertising is already penalised through the trackers. Nor are notifications: they give access to none of your data.
Precise and approximate location count only once (the heavier one).
Photos, videos, audio and legacy file access count only once.
For SMS, the heaviest counts in full, the others at half weight.
Background location, classic or through a foreground service, counts only once.
For Health Connect data, only the most sensitive tier counts.
Legacy file access only counts for apps built for Android 12 or earlier: beyond that, Android ignores it.

A tracker is a piece of code supplied by another company (often an ad network) and built into the app. It collects information about you and sends it to its own servers, in addition to the app\'s publisher.

VYLIA spots them by looking for their signatures in each app\'s code, using the public Exodus Privacy database. Each tracker costs points according to what it does; a tracker with several uses counts as the most serious one.
This is where advertising is counted: ad and profiling trackers are the heaviest. Ad targeting permissions are therefore not counted a second time.
What each category does, with examples, in the Trackers tab.
Trackers cannot cost more than %1$d points in total.
If the analysis could not be done
Until the analysis is done (or if the app could not be read), a flat %1$d points are deducted and the grade carries a “%2$s”.
Detection relies on known code names. A hidden (obfuscated) or very recent tracker can go unnoticed: “no tracker detected” is not an absolute guarantee.

What is “justified” depends on what the app does: the microphone is normal for Shazam, not for a calculator. VYLIA puts each app into one of %1$d categories, based on a list of known apps or, failing that, the category declared by the publisher.
An “Uncategorised” app gets no special treatment: every sensitive permission is considered unexpected.
Choose one of the %1$d categories to see what its purpose justifies (×%2$s), tolerates (×%3$s) or forbids (×%4$s). Any other counted permission is unexpected for it (×%5$s).
A few known apps have their own exception: %1$s.

Some combinations are typical of spyware: reading what you type, recording in the background, hiding its icon with sensitive accesses, reading the screen and drawing over other apps. They describe what an app CAN do, not what it does, but they cap its score:

A stalkerware is an app installed in secret on someone\'s phone to spy on them: messages, location, calls, photos. VYLIA compares each app with the public database of the Echap association, which lists %1$d stalkerware apps by their package names and the fingerprints of their signing certificates: an app is recognised even under another name. The check runs on the phone, without any connection. A recognised app drops to 0 and gets the “Wanted” badge.
The database is kept by volunteers and cannot know every stalkerware: finding none is not a guarantee. The capability checks below look for the rest.

Someone may have installed this app to watch you. Before uninstalling it, think about your safety: the person who installed it may notice, and the app can serve as evidence. Get help: in France, 3919 (Violences Femmes Info) is free and anonymous, and 17 is for emergencies. The stopstalkerware.org website also gives advice.

Spyware such as Pegasus, Predator or NoviSpy is sold to governments to watch journalists, activists or lawyers. VYLIA also compares each app with the public indicators of MVT, the tool of Amnesty International\'s Security Lab: %1$d campaigns are recognised by their package names or signing certificates. A recognised app drops to 0, like a stalkerware. When it is on, the shield also blocks the domains of these campaigns.

If VYLIA finds one, don\'t uninstall it right away: it is evidence. Amnesty International\'s Security Lab and Access Now\'s Digital Security Helpline (accessnow.org/help) examine phones for free and confidentially.
Badges sum up at a glance what an app does well and what deserves your attention. They do not change the score. Every badge and its rule are in the Badges tab.
Few or no sensitive permissions, and they serve the app\'s purpose; no trackers, or almost none.
A few tolerated permissions or a small number of trackers, often analytics or crash reporting.
Permissions unrelated to the app\'s purpose, or several trackers including advertising ones. Keep an eye on it.
Typically many advertising or profiling trackers, often with intrusive permissions. Look for an alternative.
Massive data collection. Replace it if you can.
Below %1$d, an app necessarily combines intrusive permissions (more than %2$d points) and significant trackers (more than %3$d points).
Permissions alone (capped at %1$d) cannot bring an app below %2$d: trackers necessarily weigh in, more than %3$d points.
Permissions alone (capped at %1$d) cannot bring an app below %2$d: trackers necessarily weigh in.

Badges sum up what an app does well and what deserves your attention, without changing its score. A card shows at most three, the most important first. Each rule below is read from the rules in force.
every sensitive permission is justified by its purpose (or tolerated and not granted).
its trackers cover at least %1$d of: %2$s.
a good-practice badge for both permissions and trackers, and no point of attention.
a red badge on both the permissions or security side and the trackers side.
at least %1$d of these, %2$s for its category%3$s: %4$s.
rule not supported by this version of VYLIA (never awarded).
None of your apps asks for it
Everything to read VYLIA: what each screen shows, how the score is calculated, the badges, and what each tracker and permission reveals about you.
Every installed app can reach part of your life: location, contacts, microphone, photos. Many also embed advertising trackers. All these accesses together form your exposure surface.
VYLIA scores each app on its permissions and trackers, and shows which data are exposed, and to how many apps.
Revoke needless permissions, remove the apps you no longer use, and replace intrusive apps with more respectful alternatives.

The shield, a local anti-tracker VPN, blocks trackers across the whole device, including in the apps you keep. And when a service works in a browser, use its web version instead of its app: the app and its trackers go away.
VYLIA compares each scan with the previous one and warns you if your exposure grows.
Measure your progress and share your score, without ever sharing your list of apps.
VYLIA describes what an app can do, not what it actually does. Everything is computed on your phone: nothing is sent.
Each app starts at 100 points and loses some for its permissions and trackers. The three icons at the top sort apps by risk, by category or by badge. Tap an app\'s icon to open its Android settings.

An overview of your phone (risk zones, anomalies, the most common trackers) and, under Tracking, the curve of your device score over time, its events and the threshold alert. The glossaries say what each tracker and each permission reveals about you.

One card per app, lowest scores first: the permissions it uses without needing them, each with its gain, and the score it would reach without them. Under Apps, the intrusive apps and those you no longer open. The glossary says what each permission is for, so you can judge whether the app really needs it.

More respectful apps, sorted by Play Store category: you choose the category and judge whether an alternative suits you, since none renders exactly the same service. The Google Play rating is shown when there is one.

Replace an app with the web version of the same service, installed by your browser as a WebAPK: the app\'s permissions and built-in trackers go away, and the DNS filtering applies to the browser. You may lose some notifications or offline use, depending on the site.

A compensating measure: the VYLIA Shield filters DNS requests on the phone and blocks trackers across the whole device, including in the apps you keep, without changing them. Private DNS is another option, handled by Android.
Your phone\'s score, your progress and your badges. Sharing makes an image of your score, progress, trackers, shield or trophies: overall figures only, never the name of an app.

Exodus Privacy is a French non-profit association that analyses Android apps and publishes the trackers they contain.

Database and API results published under the Open Database License (ODbL 1.0), contents under the Database Contents License (DbCL 1.0). VYLIA embeds an extract of this database (name, code signature, categories): apps are analysed entirely on the device. VYLIA is an independent app, neither affiliated with nor endorsed by Exodus Privacy.
Limitation: detection relies on known class names. An obfuscated or renamed SDK can go unnoticed (false negative); no tracker detected is not a guarantee.
Echap is a French non-profit association that fights technology-facilitated violence, such as spying on a partner\'s phone. It publishes stalkerware-indicators, a public database of stalkerware apps.

Database published under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (CC BY 4.0). VYLIA embeds an adapted extract (%1$d stalkerware apps, version %2$s): only their names, Android package names and signing certificate fingerprints, compared on the device. VYLIA is an independent app, neither affiliated with nor endorsed by Echap.
Limitation: the database is kept by volunteers and many stalkerware apps are probably missing. Finding none is not a guarantee.

MVT (Mobile Verification Toolkit) is the tool Amnesty International\'s Security Lab uses to find spyware such as Pegasus or Predator on the phones of journalists and activists. It publishes the indicators of these campaigns, gathered by Amnesty, Citizen Lab, Google, Lookout and other researchers.

Indicators published under the MIT licence (mvt-indicators), some by Amnesty International. VYLIA embeds an extract (%1$d campaigns with app indicators, version %2$s): package names and signing certificates, compared on the device, and the campaigns\' domains, blocked by the shield. VYLIA is an independent app, neither affiliated with nor endorsed by MVT or Amnesty International.
Limitation: these spyware apps are rare, change quickly and often leave no app behind. Finding none is not a guarantee; if you think you are targeted, ask for a full analysis of your phone.

Your exposure surface and the screens, in brief
No data collected. Your apps are analysed on your phone only.
VYLIA contains no ads, no trackers, no audience measurement tools, and sells no data.

The Internet is only used when you ask for it: to update the tracker database (the public Exodus Privacy list), the known stalkerware database (the public Echap list), the spyware indicators (MVT\'s public files) or the list of private DNS services (published with VYLIA\'s source code). Nothing about your apps is sent.
Install alerts and background scans are off by default. Once turned on, they run on the phone only, scheduled by Android.

To analyse your apps, VYLIA needs the list of installed apps (QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES): without it, there is nothing to audit. It owns this: VYLIA scores itself with the same rules as every other app, and this permission costs it points. Its page is in Scan, like the others.
Results stay on the phone. You can export, import or delete them at any time (Settings › Data management), and share your progress from Celebrate.
VYLIA is free software, licensed under the GNU GPL v3 (or any later version): you may study, modify and redistribute it under its terms. It comes with no warranty.
The VYLIA and Yogi Studio names, their logos and the app icon are not covered by the licence. The Exodus Privacy logo belongs to the Exodus Privacy association.
The VYLIA name is set in Unbounded, by The Unbounded Project Authors, under the SIL Open Font License 1.1.

The VYLIA Shield filters DNS requests with public lists, embedded in the app: Exodus Privacy (ODbL 1.0), EasyList and EasyPrivacy by the EasyList authors (GPL v3), and the AdGuard Mobile Ads filter by AdGuard (GPL v3). VYLIA is neither affiliated with nor endorsed by them.
